name: Edward Bernays

summary.text: Edward L. Bernays (1891–1995) was an American public relations counsel, a nephew of Sigmund Freud, and author of Crystallizing Public Opinion (1923) and Propaganda (1928), early works defining the field of public relations. His campaigns included the 1929 "Torches of Freedom" event promoting women's public smoking for the American Tobacco Company and, in 1953–54, a campaign for the United Fruit Company that portrayed Guatemala's government under Jacobo Arbenz as a communist threat, including press trips to Central America funded by the company. He died on March 9, 1995 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at 103. His papers (about 227,000 items) are held by the Library of Congress Manuscript Division.

facts.claim: Bernays was born in 1891 and was a nephew of Sigmund Freud; his mother was Freud's sister and his father's sister, Martha Bernays, married Freud.
facts.quote: Bernays was the nephew of Sigmund Freud. One source describes him as a "double nephew" because his mother was Freud's sister, and his father's sister, Martha Bernays Freud, married Sigmund.

facts.claim: His books Crystallizing Public Opinion (1923) and Propaganda (1928) were early efforts to define and theorize public relations, drawing on Freud, Gustave Le Bon's crowd psychology and Wilfred Trotter's theories of herd instinct.
facts.quote: Crystallizing Public Opinion (1923) and Propaganda (1928) gained special attention as early efforts to define and theorize the field of public relations.

facts.claim: In 1929, on behalf of the American Tobacco Company, Bernays arranged for women to smoke publicly in New York's Easter parade under the name "Torches of Freedom"; The New York Times of April 1, 1929 reported "Group of Girls Puff at Cigarettes as a Gesture of 'Freedom'."
facts.quote: Bernays marketed women smoking in public on behalf of the American Tobacco Company in the 1920s under the name 'Torches of Freedom.'

facts.claim: Bernays worked for the United Fruit Company during the early 1950s; a former United Fruit official recalled the company spending in excess of $100,000 a year on Bernays.
facts.quote: they were spending in excess of $100,000 a year for Edward L. Bernays.

sources.title: Watch Out for the Top Banana

facts.claim: Bernays organized trips for journalists from outlets including The New York Times, Time and The Miami Herald to Central America at United Fruit's expense, where they were introduced to company employees and selected figures and presented with a narrative of rising communist influence in Guatemala.
facts.quote: Bernays courted journalists from outlets like The New York Times, Time Magazine, and The Miami Herald, flying them to Central America on United Fruit's dime.

sources.title: Journey to Banana Land: How the United Fruit Company colluded with the CIA to Topple Guatemala's elected government
Watch Out for the Top Banana

facts.claim: Historians Stephen Schlesinger and Stephen Kinzer wrote in Bitter Fruit that by early 1954 Bernays's campaign had created an atmosphere of deep suspicion and fear in the United States regarding Guatemala; Larry Tye writes that Bernays remained a key source of information for the press through the 1954 takeover, according to his Library of Congress files.
facts.quote: By early 1954, Bernays's carefully planned campaign had created an atmosphere of deep suspicion and fear in the United States

sources.title: Watch Out for the Top Banana

facts.claim: A 2025 account of the coup notes that two United Fruit public relations agents, Thomas Corcoran and Edward L. Bernays, openly said they had promoted news stories about the Communist threat in Guatemala.
facts.quote: two Fruit Company public relations agents, Thomas Corcoran and Edward L. Bernays, bragged openly that they had promoted news stories about the Communist threat in Guatemala

facts.claim: Bernays died on March 9, 1995, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at 103.
facts.quote: Bernays died on March 9, 1995, in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He was 103 at the time.

facts.claim: The Edward L. Bernays Papers at the Library of Congress Manuscript Division (MSS12534) span 1777–1994 (bulk 1920–1990) and total about 227,000 items in 860 containers; a smaller collection (1982–1998) is held by Northeastern University.
facts.quote: The collection totals 227,000 items, 860 containers plus 54 oversize, and 160.2 linear feet.

connections.claim: Bernays served as public relations counsel to the United Fruit Company, which paid him more than $100,000 a year according to a former company official, and ran its press campaign on Guatemala in 1953–54.
connections.quote: they were spending in excess of $100,000 a year for Edward L. Bernays.

sources.title: Watch Out for the Top Banana
Journey to Banana Land: How the United Fruit Company colluded with the CIA to Topple Guatemala's elected government

connections.claim: Bernays promoted women's public smoking for the American Tobacco Company in the 1929 "Torches of Freedom" campaign and later ran a campaign to make green a fashion color to support the company's green cigarette pack.
connections.quote: When American Tobacco worried that the cigarette's famous green pack would hamper sales, Bernays launched a campaign to establish green as the fashion color of choice.

openQuestions: The site links Bernays to the CIA via the 1954 coup; no source returned states a direct relationship between Bernays and the CIA, so no CIA connection is recorded.
Claims in some accounts about a "Middle American Information Bureau" and planted Marxist literature appeared in single, non-primary sources and were left out.
Birthplace (Vienna) and the exact start date of the United Fruit engagement should be checked in Tye's The Father of Spin or Bernays's memoir.
